MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
## 1. Van name ideas (staff vote)

- **Chesterfield**
- **The Dovetail**
- **Vanessa**
- **French Polish**
- **The Mahogany Express**

## 2. Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

**B has to go first.** If he goes to A first, he arrives at 09:00 and leaves at 09:15. That puts him at B at 09:40, ten minutes after it opens. C can't be done before 11:00, so it must come last. That leaves **B, A, C** as the only order that works.

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B, unload |
| 09:05 | Finished at B (25 minutes before it opens) |
| 09:30 | Arrive A, unload (window is 09:00–10:00) |
| 09:45 | Finished at A |
| 10:25 | Arrive at C's area, take the **30-minute break** (about 10:25–10:55) |
| 11:00 | Unload at C |
| 11:15 | Finished at C |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** |

The break fits naturally into the wait for C to open.

**The catch: there's no slack at the end.** The return to the depot lands at exactly 12:00, and that depends on two assumptions:

1. **C to the depot takes 45 minutes.** You gave depot to C, not C to depot, so I've assumed the same in both directions. Check this.
2. **C lets him start unloading at 11:00 sharp, and it takes no more than 15 minutes.** Any wait at reception or difficult access makes him late.

Before tomorrow:
- Call C and ask for the van to be **first in at 11:00**, with someone ready to receive it.
- Confirm whether "back by 12:00" has any flexibility.

The morning is comfortable: there's 25 minutes spare at B and the window at A is easily met. All the risk is in the last leg.

## 3. Friendlier on-the-day text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Company] is on its way and should be with you in about [20] minutes. See you soon! Any problems, call [phone].

## 4. Evening-before text (under 160 characters)

> Hi Sam, your furniture from Oakwood Restoration arrives tomorrow 9:30-10:30. We'll text when we're on the way. Any questions, call 01234 567890.

That example is **144 characters**, which leaves some room for longer names. **Avoid emojis and curly quotes.** These switch the message to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit, so it would go as several messages. Plain apostrophes and hyphens are fine.

## 5. Three checks before handing over the furniture

1. **Condition:** look for new scratches, dents or marks on the finish, especially corners and edges, compared with how it left the workshop.
2. **Completeness:** all parts present, including shelves, keys, knobs, handles and any loose hardware.
3. **Function and stability:** drawers and doors open smoothly, the piece stands level, and nothing wobbles.

Have the customer look it over with the driver before signing. That settles any question about condition on the spot.

## 6. Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed, with the customer signing on the driver's phone or tablet.** It's quicker, harder to lose and easier to find later. Offer a paper copy to anyone who asks; some customers with valuable antiques will want one.

## 7. Proof of delivery, in one line

> **Proof of delivery is a signed, dated record showing that the item reached the right customer, at the right address, in the stated condition.**
